view: Al-ʿaṣr means time, an age, or a span of time; the oath invokes that span.
note: Sources differ over how broad the span is and whether this is the preferred meaning.

view: ʿAṣr denotes measurable, successive, irrecoverable time, unlike unlimited dahr; it can especially evoke time swiftly passing or an elapsed age.
In Arabic, al-ʿaṣr can name day, night, morning, or evening as well as time generally.
The dual al-ʿaṣrān can mean day and night; poets, including Ḥumayd ibn Thawr, attest this usage.
note: The paired phrase is a lexical argument for the day-and-night interpretation.

view: The dual al-ʿaṣrān can mean morning and evening, the two cooler parts of the day; poetry attests it.
Al-ʿaṣr means the paired span of night and day in the oath.
The oath may refer to either day or night, or to either of the two cool periods, morning and evening, without specifying one.
Al-ʿaṣr means late afternoon, the interval from the sun's decline after noon until sunset.
note: Some notes emphasize approaching night, a fading sun, or poetic evidence.

view: Al-ʿaṣr refers more narrowly to the day's final hour or the part near sunset.
note: The notes variously call it the last hour, an end of day, or the interval near sunset.

view: Al-ʿaṣr can be an hour or one period of the daytime, without a narrower time specified.
Al-ʿaṣr means evening; the afternoon prayer takes its name from that time.
note: Ibn Kathir calls the broader time interpretation better known.

view: An Arabic poetic use of ʿaṣr denotes an age, and variant vowel forms also designate a specific time.
A poem contrasts a day, month, and age to illustrate the different scales of time.
The root ʿ-ṣ-r means pressing or squeezing out liquid, as from cloth or grapes; related nouns name the press, its place, and its stones.

The squeezing image extends to time as the span in which events are worked and turned, or an age in which experience and hardship press out a person's essence; late afternoon is the day pressed toward its end.
The afternoon prayer is named for its time, or for its being deferred from the start of that time.

Related Arabic forms include juice pressed from grapes, rain-bearing clouds, rain-making people, and a wind or column of dust twisting upward; the Qur'an uses these roots for squeezing, clouds, and a whirlwind.
Metaphorical ʿaṣr also conveys confinement, restraint, pressure, or extraction; some related forms convey lineage, a group, rain, bestowal, or taxing.
Dahr can denote the universe's whole duration, a long span, or a remaining life; zamān can mean the whole or a part of it.
In Turkish, asr commonly means time, the present era, or a span of eighty or a hundred years.
The opening wāw is the oath particle, with humanity's loss as its answer; one account says time thereby bears witness.
note: The notes differ in whether they describe the particle as an oath or witness.

view: The oath particle magnifies what is sworn by and moves from a perceptible reality to a moral truth.
The oath by time confirms the following assertion and honors a created sign of God's power and knowledge.
The definite article can be generic, gathering the word's senses, or refer to a known particular time, immediately suggesting the Prophet's era to his first audience.
With no proof restricting it, the oath can encompass all senses of ʿaṣr, including time broadly, parts of day and night, and even refuge.
note: Al-Tabari and Elmalılı favor breadth; al-Nahhas explicitly adds refuge.

view: Al-ʿaṣr is best read as the age or time generally, especially because the sūra's universal message suits that scope.
note: Jishumi prefers time over Ali's misfortunes; other notes name al-Tabari, Ibn Qayyim, or the majority.

view: The linguistic sense 'time in general' is challenged as insufficiently apparent.
Other Qur'anic opening oaths name specific phases of day or night, so this ʿaṣr likely names a particular time; a late-afternoon oath would be distinctive among early Meccan oaths.
The oath invokes the Lord of Time or Lord of the age, with the object understood elliptically.
The oath invokes the afternoon prayer, identified as the middle prayer and praised as especially excellent.
note: Some notes point to 2:238 or Hafsa's codex; Study Quran notes other identifications of the middle prayer.

view: Reports identify the middle prayer as ʿAṣr; Hafsa's codex and a reported reading of 5:106 are also cited for the identification.
note: The sources present different forms of evidence for this identification.

view: A Prophetic report compares missing the afternoon prayer to losing one's family and property.
The afternoon prayer deserves emphasis because trade, livelihood, work, and end-of-day accounts make it hard to maintain.
The afternoon prayer closes the day's worship as repentance closes deeds; the oath magnifies it and urges prayer, turning loss toward profit.
God may swear by a human prayer because it is His noble prescription, not merely a human deed.
A story links a woman's confessed adultery, killing of her child, and sale of the child's remains in vinegar to neglect of ʿAṣr prayer; another commentator rejects this report as unreliable.
note: Al-Alusi rejects the story attributed to a prominent transmitter.

view: A Prophetic warning says a false oath after the afternoon prayer brings God's displeasure and loss of His regard or speech on Judgment Day.
The oath can invoke the time when Adam was created on Friday afternoon.
The oath may invoke the Prophet's era, honored by renewed prophethood and the Prophet, his community, and their revelation.
note: The cited spans vary from the Prophet's lifetime to his community's era through the Resurrection.

view: The oath may cover each person's lifetime, the span in which each must act.
Some narrations identify ʿaṣr with the Mahdi's era, when truth fully prevails.
Some take ʿaṣr as the end times or final era of human history.
The Prophet's era fits the following account of loss and the exception of those who follow truth, since Islam then arose and truth appeared over falsehood.
The Prophet's era can be called the afternoon of human history; earlier peoples worked in its morning and midday, whereas his community is the final workers.
A parable gives the final group of workers, from afternoon to sunset, double pay after earlier groups object; this supports likening the Prophet's community to the late part of history.
A report says the Prophet's community will last a day if upright, or half a day otherwise.
Other oaths by the Prophet's place and life are compared with an oath by his era.
The Prophet's mission began amid ignorance, injustice, and religious disorder; Qur'anic revelation and his call opened a path of reform, salvation, and a new historical era.
His lifetime's era passed through struggle and then conquest, with guidance spreading and truth distinguished from falsehood.
The Muhammadic era from the Hijra to the end of time brings earlier prophetic eras' aims to fruition.
Time's unbroken continuity encompasses the Prophet's sainthood, prophethood, mission, and caliphate, supported by reports of his pre-eternal prophetic status and creation for his sake.
Time's changing conditions, wonders, blessings, and opposites reveal the Creator's power and make the oath an invitation to reflect.
note: Several notes mention alternating night and day; some reject blaming time for harms.

view: The afternoon's fading light and approaching night display divine power, like forenoon or dawn in other oaths.
Late afternoon closes work, gathers daily gains, and reveals whether the day was profitable; it can evoke a life near its end and the approaching Judgment.
note: Al-Hasan adds dependents and creditors; Robinson stresses merchants counting earnings.

view: Morning can figure resurrection while evening or afternoon figures death or the world's destruction; remaining daylight calls for repentance and a trade without loss.
Afternoon recalls the solar-earth cycle, daily work and household rhythms, divine blessings, and death after life's stages.
The afternoon oath complements oaths by forenoon or dawn, setting decline beside rising light.
note: Razi also contrasts reassurance in the previous sūra with warning here.

view: The oath gathers signs invoked in other Qur'anic oaths by dawn, sun, moon, night, day, and forenoon.
The oath by ʿaṣr can allude to time's squeezing or confinement, which suits the following loss, while also allowing gain through faith and good works.
The name ʿAṣr evokes extraction of an essence, matching the sūra's distinction between the saved and the doomed.
The choice of ʿaṣr over dahr avoids echoing claims that time destroys, while honoring time as a blessing.
Time is a blessing and setting for deeds; people, not time, cause their loss by wasting it or doing wrong, despite the habit of blaming time for misfortune.
note: Muhammad Abdu connects the mistake with alleged afternoon gatherings; Bint al-Shati disputes that alleged custom.

view: A report forbids reviling time and says God is time or al-dahr.
God is the true agent of change manifested through time, while people wrongly treat time as the agent.
The nature of time is puzzling: past and future are absent and the present indivisible; thinkers debate whether time exists, is imagined, or is known immediately or by abstraction.
A final instant of repentance or right action can redeem years of waste and bring eternal salvation, showing time's immense worth.
Night and day offer opportunity to remember and thank God, and their alternation and changing light and temperature show His dominion and wisdom.
Human life is a rapidly spent investment: each unproductive day or breath reduces what remains, and faith and good works turn that loss into gain.
note: The notes include poetry about passing days and death, and Farahi's merchant with melting ice.

view: Only the present moment can be shaped: the past cannot return, the future is uncertain, and today's duty cannot safely be deferred.
note: A Sufi use of the present aims at the afterlife, whereas a worldly hedonist aims at pleasure.

view: A person should be a child of the moment, using the present for good in the afterlife.
The speed of time offers hope: brief self-discipline can win eternal pleasure, while being lured by worldly pleasure forfeits it.
The oath evokes past nations' exact recompense: virtue brought ascendancy, whereas oppression and disorder brought destruction after a respite; later people face the same law.
The afternoon might have been a customary time of harmful talk, giving the oath force as a correction of blame placed on time; this customary-gathering claim is disputed.
note: Bint al-Shati says evening may fit gatherings better and objectionable talk can occur at any time.

view: A time or place can be honored because of those within it: the oath's honor of the Prophet's era intensifies the loss of those who reject him.
The oath's object may be any of several periods; each manifests divine action and makes the oath meaningful through context, addition, or a shared referent.
The sūra opens with a single-member oath followed by a rebuke and a believer exception; its three clauses rhyme.
Oaths by prayer times may preserve liturgical experience and give a hymn-like tone; this hymn-like reading is disputed.
note: The Corpus Coranicum commentator finds no such resonance here.

view: Qur'anic oaths may draw on a pre-Islamic seer expression, a relationship said to need more study.
Ali is attributed an expanded recitation invoking time's vicissitudes and saying humans remain in loss until time's end; another version, also ascribed to Ibn Masud, adds only the duration of loss.
note: The sound standard-codex reading is preferred by al-Thaʿlabi.

view: The sound reading follows the general reciters and standard codices, rather than the expanded readings attributed to Ali and Ibn Masud.
Salam's reading gives ṣād in al-ʿaṣr a kasra, alongside a kasra in al-ṣabr; it is explained as vowel transfer at a pause, though reports also allow connected recitation.
note: Razi offers stopping for breath; al-Hudhali reports further words and continuous recitation.

view: Transferring a final consonant's vowel backward at pause marks inflection, avoids adjacent vowelless letters, and preserves pause-sukūn; Arabic poetry supports it, and transfer can involve ḍamma.
The sūra is Meccan, although reports also classify it as Medinan; its three verses are agreed upon.
note: Ibn Abbas and other authorities are cited for Meccan classification; Mujahid, Qatada, and Muqatil for Medinan.

view: The sūra is placed shortly after Sūra 94 in revelation order.
One verse division joins this oath to verse 2; another treats the oath as an independent verse, as with other opening oaths.
note: Spitaler's Medina II joins; Neuwirth prefers a separate verse.

view: A report promises reciters of Sūrat al-ʿAṣr patience and companionship with the people of truth on Resurrection Day.
Ubayy is reported to have recited the sūra to the Prophet and asked its interpretation; a related report says God swears by the day's end.
A report interprets the sūra's phrases through Abu Jahl and Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali; Ali ibn Abd Allah ibn Abbas repeated these identifications in a sermon.
Before his conversion, Amr ibn al-As reportedly recited al-ʿAṣr to Musaylima, who answered with an unimpressive parody about the small, catlike wabr; al-Kharaʾiti also transmitted the story.
Two Companions reportedly recited Sūrat al-ʿAṣr to one another when they met and exchanged greetings before parting.
note: Qutb reads the custom as renewing commitment to the sūra's guidance.

view: At Umar's stabbing, Abd al-Rahman led Fajr and recited al-ʿAṣr with al-Naṣr.
Al-Shafiʿi reportedly said that reflection on this brief sūra would suffice people; related reports say it gathers all Qur'anic sciences even if nothing else were revealed.
The brief sūra summarizes the Qur'an's religious and moral program, the Muslim community's identity, and the path of faith, righteous action, truth, and patience.
note: Some notes stress the community's mutual counsel and that faith alone is insufficient.

view: People are in loss when they neglect God's rights, follow desire, or fail to fear Him.
Affliction falls on prophets, then saints, then the best people in descending order of excellence.
Affliction is God's whip driving His servants toward Him.
The sūra distinguishes those saved from those doomed and urges leaving fleeting gains for lasting salvation.
The sūra's clauses can be mapped to knowledge of God and the afterlife, worship, and patience that avoids doubt and harm.
note: Al-Ghazali compares the Qur'an to a sea with six minerals: God, attributes and acts, afterlife, worship, harmful doubts, and lessons from saved and ruined.

view: The sūra begins with the ruined and saved because preventing harm precedes securing benefit.
The basmala presents all things as perishing except God, whose mercy reaches all and whose completed gifts distinguish His allies.
After al-Takathur's warning against rivalry, worldly abundance, and Hell, this sūra distinguishes believer from unbeliever and shows how good action prevents loss.
note: Several notes link waste of life's blessing to worldly accumulation.

view: A comparison with another exception clause says this sūra further requires mutual exhortation to truth and patience, preventing loss of reward.

For an oath not to speak to someone for an ʿaṣr, Malik takes the period as a year; al-Shafiʿi takes it as an hour unless otherwise intended, while Ibn al-Arabi largely prefers the hour with a qualified allowance for plausible Arab usage.
note: The disagreement concerns the duration conveyed by ʿaṣr and the force of the swearer's intent.

view: A generic definite noun can be qualified by exceptions; an analogy with this sūra supports the rule that killing any protected life is forbidden except for a valid legal cause.
Reading the sūra after al-Takathur makes time the blessing wasted in competition for more and a gift for which people must answer.
Every generation declines a degree from the previous one as the reading applies to individuals and all human history.
An interpretation loads time with philosophical or mystical meaning; Bint al-Shati rejects such elaboration in favor of the Qur'an's accessible signs of night and day.
Al-Razi's magnification of the age draws on extraordinary change, the worth of life's final moment, and time's rank over space; he also argues for a particular time, prayer, and prophetic era.
Human loss is grave because a servant sins against the Lord despite immense benefaction; the indefinite form may suggest a loss beyond ordinary usage.
Whoever hears God's name gives wealth for it, trusting God to make the final outcome good.
Whoever knows God's name does not prefer self over it, because intimacy is found only with it.
Whoever accompanies God's name offers even the spirit for it, having received eternal life through it.
